title: The final salok: air, water, earth
hook: pavan guru paanee pitaa maataa dharat mahat: air the Guru, water the father, earth the great mother; day and night the nurses (Japji, salok)

segments.voice: Yesterday, sabad, in the last pauri: the word is minted. Today, the short verse that closes the whole Japji.

The first few minutes of your life. Before you had a name, before you knew anyone's face, three things met you. Air rushed into your lungs, and you cried. Water: you'd floated in it for months, and someone washed you in it. Then you were laid down, held, on something solid. Air, water, ground: there before any teacher, any parent's voice, any word, and there again every morning since, without being asked. After thirty-eight stanzas of climbing, the Japji doesn't end at the top of the ladder. It ends with one short verse that comes all the way back down to these three.
screen: `YOUR FIRST MINUTES.` → `AIR, WATER, GROUND.` → `THE JAPJI COMES BACK DOWN.`

segments.voice: The Japji opened with a salok, a short verse, before the first pauri: aad sach, true in the beginning. It closes with one more: pavan guroo paanee pitaa maataa dharat mahat. Air is the Guru, water the father, earth the great mother. Air as Guru is worth a moment. The breath carries every word, every hymn, every sound of the Name; without air, no teaching reaches anyone. Then: divas raat due daaee daaiaa, khelai sagal jagat. Day and night are the two nurses, a woman and a man who care for a child, and in their lap the whole world plays. A family picture of creation: parents, nurses, and all of us, children, playing. Then the tone turns serious. Good and bad deeds are read out in the presence of Dharam, the righteous judge. By their own actions, some come near, some stay far. And the last lines: those who remembered the Name have finished their hard work and gone. Nanak says, their faces shine, and many others are set free along with them. Many Sikhs today quote pavan guroo paanee pitaa when they speak about caring for the earth: if the air is your teacher and the earth your mother, you don't treat them like trash. And notice where the Japji leaves you. Not in a far realm, but right here, breathing, drinking, standing on the ground.
screen: `PAVAN GUROO — AIR IS THE GURU.` · `WATER THE FATHER, EARTH THE MOTHER.` · `DAY AND NIGHT, THE TWO NURSES.` · `FACES SHINE, AND OTHERS GO FREE.` · then, large: `AIR, WATER, EARTH.`

segments.voice: If you can, open a window or step outside; if not, stay where you are, and breathe in slowly, feeling the air come in, the Guru in the salok's picture. Take a sip of water if you have some, then press your feet into the floor, into the earth beneath the building. Stay with the breath, letting air, water and earth hold you, the way they did in your first minutes.
Pavan, air, the breath that carries every word. The short verse that closes the Japji: air the Guru, water the father, earth the great mother, day and night the nurses, and faces that shine.
Your line: air, water, earth. Teacher, father and mother, all around you. That's day two hundred thirty.

screen: `DAY 230 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: CAMP 4 CLOSE: THE WHOLE JAPJI.`

trapdoor: what you thought: a nature poem tacked on the end.
what it means: creation as a family that raises us, a reckoning of deeds, and faces that shine with many freed alongside.
what a scholar hears: a close version of this salok appears later in the Granth credited to Guru Angad; daaee and daaiaa are a female and a male nurse.
